\section[triste]{triste — sad}

\label{lesson:FR-C56-triste}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for sadness, then the French for happy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: triste}
\textbf{triste} — \textquotedblleft{}sad\textquotedblright{}. The adjective beside \textbf{la tristesse}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{triste} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{tristis}, \textquotedblleft{}sad, gloomy\textquotedblright{} — inherited. (EtymDB 2.1)
\end{cousinweb}

\section[content]{content — pleased, glad}

\label{lesson:FR-C56-content}

\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: content}
\textbf{content} — \textquotedblleft{}pleased, glad\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{content} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{contentus}, \textquotedblleft{}satisfied\textquotedblright{}, the past participle of \emph{continere}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold together\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short) — taken from written Latin; Old French already had it (EtymDB 2.1).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[le grand-père]{le grand-père — a grandfather}

\label{lesson:FR-C56-grand-pere}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for pleased, then the French for a daughter; a girl.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: le grand-père}
\textbf{le grand-père} — \textquotedblleft{}a grandfather\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{grand-père} — built from the French word for \textquotedblleft{}big, great\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{grandis} (EtymDB 2.1), and \emph{père}, \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{grandfather} copied the French pattern.
\end{cousinweb}
